title: Neuropharmacology I: Excitability, Seizures & Sedation
summary: Drugs that tune neuronal excitability: antiseizure medications, sedatives and anesthetics.

lessons.title: Sodium & Calcium Channel Drugs

levels.kid:
Brain cells talk with tiny electric sparks. A seizure is when too many cells spark all at once, like a crowd all shouting together.

Each spark needs little doors on the cell to open. Some doors let in salt bits called sodium. Some let in calcium.

Some seizure medicines work like a gentle hand on those doors. They keep the doors from flapping open too fast. The cells can still talk, but they can't all shout at the same time.

Doctors pick the medicine that fits the kind of seizure, a bit like picking the right key for a lock.
levels.hs:
Neurons fire **action potentials** when voltage-gated sodium (Na+) channels open and Na+ rushes in. Calcium (Ca2+) channels help trigger neurotransmitter release and, in some brain circuits, rhythmic firing. A seizure is excessive, synchronized firing, so many antiseizure medications (ASMs) calm these channels.

**Sodium channel blockers**
- Examples: phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide.
- They hold sodium channels in their "resting-after-firing" (inactivated) state longer.
- Key idea: they work best on neurons firing very fast, like during a seizure, so normal activity is mostly spared. This is called **use-dependent block**.
- Used mainly for focal (partial) seizures.

**Calcium channel drugs**
- **Ethosuximide** blocks T-type calcium channels in the thalamus. These channels drive the 3-per-second spike-and-wave rhythm of **absence seizures** (brief staring spells), so ethosuximide is a first choice for them.
- **Gabapentin** and **pregabalin** bind a helper part of calcium channels (the α2δ subunit) and reduce neurotransmitter release. They are used for focal seizures and nerve pain.

**A twist:** sodium blockers like carbamazepine can make absence and myoclonic seizures worse. Choosing the right drug depends on the seizure type.
levels.college:
**Voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav)** cycle through resting, open and inactivated states. Classic ASMs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine/eslicarbazepine) bind preferentially to the **fast-inactivated** state and slow its recovery. Because high-frequency discharges leave more channels inactivated, block accumulates during seizures: **use- (frequency-) dependent block**. **Lacosamide** instead enhances **slow inactivation**, a distinct conformational process, which is why it may add benefit on top of a classic blocker (though shared side effects such as dizziness and diplopia add up).

**T-type Ca2+ channels (Cav3)** in thalamic relay and reticular neurons generate low-threshold spikes that produce burst firing. In absence epilepsy, thalamocortical oscillations yield 3 Hz generalized spike-wave discharges. **Ethosuximide** reduces T-type current; valproate also has some effect. Ethosuximide does not protect against generalized tonic-clonic seizures, so it fits pure childhood absence epilepsy.

**α2δ ligands**: gabapentin and pregabalin bind α2δ-1 auxiliary subunits of presynaptic high-voltage-activated Ca2+ channels, reducing trafficking and release of glutamate and substance P. Despite their names, they do not act on GABA receptors.

**Broad-spectrum agents** combine mechanisms: valproate (Na+ block, T-type Ca2+ reduction, increased GABA), topiramate and zonisamide (Na+ and Ca2+ effects plus others).

**Clinical selection**
- Focal seizures: lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide.
- Absence: ethosuximide, valproate, lamotrigine.
- Generalized (including myoclonic): valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine (may worsen myoclonus).
- **Aggravation**: carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and gabapentin/pregabalin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures.
- **Dravet syndrome** (loss-of-function SCN1A in inhibitory interneurons): sodium channel blockers worsen seizures because they further silence the inhibitory cells.
levels.phd:
**Structural pharmacology.** Classic ASMs bind within the inner pore of Nav channels, overlapping the local anesthetic site formed by residues on the S6 segments of domains III and IV (a conserved phenylalanine on DIV-S6 is critical). Cryo-EM structures of human Nav1.7 and Nav1.5 with bound blockers support a model where drugs access the pore through membrane fenestrations (hydrophobic pathway) or the open activation gate (hydrophilic pathway). State-dependent affinity follows the **modulated receptor hypothesis**: higher affinity for inactivated states produces voltage- and frequency-dependence.

**Kinetic signatures differ.** Phenytoin and carbamazepine have slow binding and unbinding kinetics compared with lidocaine-like agents; lamotrigine combines Nav block with effects on HCN-related dendritic excitability. Lacosamide's enhancement of slow inactivation occurs over seconds, selectively damping sustained depolarization (for example, paroxysmal depolarizing shifts) while sparing brief bursts.

**Channelopathies reshape pharmacology.** SCN1A loss-of-function (Dravet) reduces Nav1.1 in parvalbumin-positive interneurons, so further Na+ block reduces inhibition and worsens seizures. In contrast, SCN2A and SCN8A gain-of-function epileptic encephalopathies can respond strikingly to high-intensity sodium blockade, a clear example of genotype-guided precision therapy. Developmental timing matters too: SCN2A variants with early-onset gain-of-function differ from later-onset loss-of-function variants associated with autism.

**Thalamocortical circuits.** Absence seizures arise from interactions between the reticular thalamic nucleus (GABAergic), thalamic relay cells and cortex (the somatosensory "cortical focus" theory from rodent models). T-type Cav3.1 knockout mice resist spike-wave discharges, while Cav3.2 gain-of-function variants appear in some human idiopathic generalized epilepsy cohorts. Ethosuximide's T-type block in relay neurons may be supplemented by cortical actions, an unresolved question.

**α2δ biology.** α2δ-1 also acts as a thrombospondin receptor in synaptogenesis and associates with NMDA receptors, suggesting gabapentinoid effects extend beyond Ca2+ channel trafficking. Precise mechanism attribution remains debated.
levels.expert:
**Choosing a sodium channel drug at the bedside.** First, classify the epilepsy. Giving carbamazepine to a teenager whose "staring spells" are actually absence or whose morning jerks are juvenile myoclonic epilepsy can make things worse. Look at the EEG: 3 Hz generalized spike-wave or polyspike-wave pushes you toward broad-spectrum agents.

**Practical points an attending checks**
- **HLA-B*15:02** screening before carbamazepine (and caution with oxcarbazepine and phenytoin) in patients with Asian ancestry, because it strongly predicts Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis. HLA-A*31:01 relates to carbamazepine hypersensitivity in several populations.
- **Phenytoin**: nonlinear (saturable, zero-order) kinetics, so small adjustments can produce large level changes; highly protein-bound, so with low albumin or renal failure measure the free level. Chronic effects include gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarse features, cerebellar atrophy and osteomalacia. IV fosphenytoin is preferred over IV phenytoin (less tissue injury, "purple glove" syndrome).
- **Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine**: hyponatremia (oxcarbazepine more), autoinduction of carbamazepine metabolism over the first weeks, leukopenia.
- **Lamotrigine**: very slow titration to cut rash risk; slower still with valproate.
- **Lacosamide**: PR prolongation, so get an ECG in conduction disease.
- **Toxicity pattern** for this class: dizziness, diplopia, nystagmus, ataxia. That cerebellar picture in a patient on phenytoin is a level check, not a stroke workup first.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Seizure prophylaxis after traumatic brain injury and after supratentorial surgery is common; levetiracetam has largely replaced phenytoin because of fewer interactions and no level monitoring, though evidence for long-term prophylaxis benefit is limited. Prophylaxis reduces early posttraumatic seizures (first week) but does not prevent later epilepsy.

**Pitfall:** escalating sodium blockers in an infant with Dravet syndrome. Prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizures in the first year should prompt SCN1A testing.

keyPoints: Seizures are excessive, synchronized neuronal firing; many ASMs target Na+ or Ca2+ channels.
Phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine and oxcarbazepine stabilize fast-inactivated Na+ channels (use-dependent block); lacosamide enhances slow inactivation.
Ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels: first-line for absence seizures.
Gabapentin and pregabalin bind the α2δ subunit and reduce transmitter release; they do not act on GABA receptors.
Na+ channel blockers can worsen absence, myoclonic seizures and Dravet syndrome.

test.q: What does use-dependent block mean for sodium channel antiseizure drugs?
choices: They block resting and firing channels equally
They work best on neurons firing rapidly
test.explain: Rapid firing leaves more channels inactivated, which these drugs bind, so block builds during seizures and normal firing is mostly spared.

test.q: Which drug is a first-line choice for childhood absence seizures?
test.explain: Ethosuximide blocks thalamic T-type Ca2+ channels that drive 3 Hz spike-wave discharges. The others can worsen absence seizures.

test.q: Lacosamide differs from carbamazepine because it mainly:
choices: Enhances slow inactivation of Na+ channels
Blocks T-type Ca2+ channels in the thalamus
Binds the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A
Blocks NMDA receptors at the glutamate site
test.explain: Lacosamide enhances slow inactivation; classic blockers bind the fast-inactivated state.

test.q: Gabapentin and pregabalin act by binding:
choices: The benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors
The α2δ subunit of calcium channels
The inner pore of voltage-gated sodium channels
test.explain: Despite the name, gabapentin does not act on GABA receptors; it binds α2δ subunits and reduces transmitter release.

test.q: A sodium channel blocker is most likely to WORSEN which condition?
test.explain: In Dravet (SCN1A loss of function in inhibitory interneurons), further Na+ block reduces inhibition and worsens seizures.

test.q: Which EEG pattern is classic for absence seizures?
test.explain: Absence seizures show 3-per-second generalized spike-and-wave discharges.

test.q: Phenytoin has zero-order (saturable) kinetics. What is the clinical consequence?
choices: Levels stay fixed once a steady state is reached
Small dose changes can cause large level changes
Each dose change takes months to affect the level
It has no drug interactions because it is not metabolized
test.explain: Once metabolism saturates, a small increase can raise the level disproportionately, causing toxicity.

test.q: Which brain structure contains the T-type calcium channels that drive absence seizure rhythms?
test.explain: Thalamocortical circuits generate the 3 Hz rhythm; T-type channels in thalamic neurons drive burst firing.

test.q: Before carbamazepine in patients with Asian ancestry, screen for HLA-B*___ to reduce SJS/TEN risk.
test.explain: HLA-B*15:02 strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.

test.q: Name the subunit of calcium channels that gabapentin binds (Greek letters allowed as words).
test.explain: Gabapentinoids bind the α2δ (alpha-2-delta) auxiliary subunit.

test.q: Classic signs of sodium channel blocker toxicity are:
test.explain: A cerebellar picture (nystagmus, ataxia, double vision) is typical of toxicity with phenytoin and carbamazepine.

kidTest.q: A seizure is when brain cells…
kidTest.explain: Too many brain cells firing together causes a seizure.

kidTest.q: Many seizure medicines work on tiny ___ on brain cells.
kidTest.explain: Channels are like doors that let sodium or calcium in.

kidTest.q: One kind of door lets in salty bits called ___.
kidTest.explain: Sodium channels let sodium in to make a spark.

kidTest.q: Do doctors use the same medicine for every seizure?
choices: Yes, always the very same medicine
No, they pick one that fits the seizure type
Seizures never need any medicine at all
kidTest.explain: Different seizure types need different medicines.

kidTest.q: Seizure medicines try to stop cells from…
kidTest.explain: Cells still talk normally; the medicine stops them from all firing together.

advancedTest.q: Why might very high-intensity sodium channel blockade help some SCN8A or SCN2A encephalopathies but harm SCN1A Dravet syndrome?
choices: SCN1A encodes a voltage-gated calcium channel rather than a sodium channel
Gain-of-function variants increase Na+ current in excitatory neurons, whereas Dravet reduces Na+ current in inhibitory interneurons
Dravet syndrome is not genetic, so channel blockers simply act on the scarred hippocampus instead of a channel
SCN8A and SCN2A variants are expressed mainly in the liver, where they speed up clearance of these drugs
advancedTest.explain: Genotype predicts direction: blocking excess current helps gain-of-function; further silencing interneurons worsens loss-of-function Dravet.

advancedTest.q: A patient on phenytoin has low albumin and a 'normal' total level but nystagmus and ataxia. Best next step?
choices: Increase phenytoin because a normal total level underestimates its effect
Switch to carbamazepine to avoid protein binding issues
Order brain imaging in place of a free-drug level
advancedTest.explain: Low albumin raises the free fraction; total levels underestimate active drug, so measure free phenytoin.

advancedTest.q: According to the modulated receptor hypothesis, frequency-dependent block occurs because drug affinity is highest for:
advancedTest.explain: High affinity for open/inactivated states means block accumulates when channels cycle rapidly.

advancedTest.q: Antiseizure prophylaxis after traumatic brain injury reduces which posttraumatic seizures: early or late? (type one word)
advancedTest.explain: Prophylaxis cuts first-week (early) seizures but does not prevent later posttraumatic epilepsy.

lessons.title: GABAergic Drugs

levels.kid:
Your brain has a "go" signal and a "slow down" signal. The main slow-down signal is a chemical called GABA.

When GABA lands on a brain cell, it opens a little door that lets in tiny bits that make the cell calmer. A calm cell is less likely to spark.

Some medicines help GABA do its job better. They are like turning up the volume on the "shh, slow down" voice. Doctors use them to stop long seizures, to help people relax before surgery, and to help muscles that are too tight.

But too much slowing down can make people very sleepy, so doctors watch carefully.
levels.hs:
**GABA** (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter. Its main receptor, **GABA-A**, is a channel that lets chloride (Cl-) ions into the neuron. That usually makes the inside more negative, so the neuron is less likely to fire.

**Drugs that boost GABA-A**
- **Benzodiazepines** (lorazepam, diazepam, midazolam): bind a separate site on the receptor and make GABA open the channel **more often**. Used to stop prolonged seizures (status epilepticus), for anxiety, muscle spasm and sedation before procedures.
- **Barbiturates** (phenobarbital): keep the channel open **longer**. At high levels they can open it even without GABA, which makes them more dangerous.
- **Propofol**: an IV anesthetic that strongly enhances GABA-A.

**Drugs that raise GABA levels**
- **Vigabatrin** blocks the enzyme that breaks GABA down (used for infantile spasms).
- **Tiagabine** blocks GABA reuptake.

**GABA-B** is a different receptor that works through G proteins. **Baclofen** activates it and treats spasticity (tight muscles) from spinal cord injury, MS or cerebral palsy.

**Safety:** these drugs can cause sleepiness and slowed breathing, especially combined with other sedating medicines. **Flumazenil** blocks the benzodiazepine site and can reverse benzodiazepine effects in specific situations.
levels.college:
**GABA-A receptors** are pentameric ligand-gated Cl- channels, most commonly two α, two β and one γ2 subunit. GABA binds at the β-α interfaces; **benzodiazepines** bind the α-γ2 interface and act as positive allosteric modulators, increasing **opening frequency** (and GABA affinity). They require GABA and have a ceiling effect, giving a wider safety margin. Benzodiazepine sensitivity depends on α1, α2, α3 or α5 paired with γ2; α4 and α6 receptors are insensitive.

**Subunit pharmacology**: α1 mediates sedation and amnesia (and is targeted by "Z-drugs" such as zolpidem); α2/α3 mediate anxiolysis and muscle relaxation; α5 (hippocampus) relates to memory. **Extrasynaptic** δ-containing receptors produce tonic inhibition and are highly sensitive to neurosteroids.

**Barbiturates** increase **open duration** and at higher concentrations directly gate the channel; they also inhibit AMPA receptors. No ceiling, so respiratory depression risk is high. **Propofol** and **etomidate** act on β-subunit sites; **neurosteroids** (for example, allopregnanolone itself, given as brexanolone, and its analog ganaxolone for CDKL5 deficiency disorder) bind transmembrane sites.

**GABA metabolism**: GABA is made from glutamate by glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD, needs pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6) and broken down by GABA transaminase. **Vigabatrin** irreversibly inhibits GABA-T (infantile spasms, especially tuberous sclerosis), with risk of permanent concentric visual field loss. **Tiagabine** inhibits GAT-1 reuptake. **Valproate** also raises GABA.

**GABA-B** receptors are Gi/o-coupled metabotropic heterodimers: postsynaptically they open GIRK K+ channels; presynaptically they inhibit Ca2+ channels. **Baclofen** is a GABA-B agonist for spasticity, also given intrathecally by pump.

**Status epilepticus**: benzodiazepine first (IV lorazepam, IM midazolam, or rectal/intranasal diazepam/midazolam), then a second-line agent (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate), then anesthetic infusions if refractory.

**Reversal**: flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine-site antagonist; in chronic users it can precipitate seizures.
levels.phd:
**Why benzodiazepines fail as seizures persist.** In prolonged status epilepticus, synaptic γ2-containing GABA-A receptors are internalized via clathrin-mediated endocytosis, reducing benzodiazepine sensitivity within tens of minutes, while NMDA and AMPA receptors traffic to the surface. Extrasynaptic δ-receptors are not internalized similarly, motivating neurosteroid strategies.

**Chloride homeostasis.** GABA-A responses depend on the Cl- gradient set by NKCC1 (loading) and KCC2 (extrusion). In immature neurons, high NKCC1 makes GABA depolarizing; KCC2 upregulation produces the developmental "GABA switch." Neonatal seizures respond poorly to phenobarbital partly for this reason. After injury, KCC2 downregulation (via BDNF-TrkB signaling and calpain cleavage) can make GABA depolarizing in epileptic tissue, peritumoral cortex and the spinal dorsal horn in neuropathic pain. Bumetanide (an NKCC1 inhibitor) failed as a neonatal seizure add-on in the NEMO trial, partly due to poor brain penetration and ototoxicity.

**Structural insight.** Cryo-EM structures of α1β2γ2 receptors bound to diazepam, alprazolam, phenobarbital and propofol identified the classical extracellular α+/γ- benzodiazepine site, transmembrane β+/α- anesthetic sites, and a second low-affinity diazepam site in the transmembrane domain, helping explain biphasic effects.

**Tolerance and dependence.** Chronic benzodiazepine exposure produces subunit composition changes, uncoupling between allosteric and GABA sites, and glutamatergic adaptation, explaining tolerance to anticonvulsant and sedative effects and the risk of withdrawal seizures on abrupt discontinuation.

**Subtype-selective goals.** α2/α3-preferring modulators aimed to separate anxiolysis from sedation; human results have been mixed. Positive allosteric modulators of α5 or negative modulators of α5 (for cognition) illustrate how subunit-targeted pharmacology remains an active research frontier.
levels.expert:
**Status epilepticus is a clock.** The most common failure is underdosing or delaying the benzodiazepine, then rushing to a second agent. Give an adequate weight-based benzodiazepine dose promptly by whatever route works (IV, IM, intranasal, buccal), and start the second-line agent if seizures continue. The ESETT trial showed levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate perform similarly as second-line drugs, so choose based on the patient: valproate avoided in pregnancy, liver disease and suspected mitochondrial disorders (POLG); fosphenytoin needs cardiac monitoring for hypotension and arrhythmia.

**Refractory status** means anesthetic infusions (midazolam, propofol, or pentobarbital) with continuous EEG, intubation and blood pressure support. Watch for **propofol infusion syndrome** (metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, rising triglycerides, cardiac failure) with prolonged high-rate infusions.

**Respiratory safety.** Benzodiazepines plus opioids, alcohol or other sedatives synergistically depress breathing; elderly patients and those with sleep apnea or neuromuscular weakness are most vulnerable. Paradoxical agitation can occur in children and older adults.

**Flumazenil caveats.** Reverses benzodiazepine sedation after procedures, but in patients on chronic benzodiazepines or with a mixed overdose involving a seizure-provoking drug it can precipitate seizures. Its duration may be shorter than the benzodiazepine's, so re-sedation occurs.

**Baclofen.** Intrathecal pumps used for severe spasticity are a neurosurgical device. Abrupt interruption (catheter kink, pump failure, refill error) causes **baclofen withdrawal**: rebound spasticity, itching, fever, autonomic instability, seizures and potentially rhabdomyolysis and death. Treat as an emergency: restore intrathecal delivery, oral baclofen and benzodiazepines as bridges. Overdose causes hypotonia, coma and respiratory depression.

**Vigabatrin.** Baseline and regular visual field assessment; vision loss is irreversible. Still worthwhile for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis because it can be dramatically effective.

keyPoints: GABA-A is a pentameric Cl- channel; activation usually hyperpolarizes neurons.
Benzodiazepines increase opening frequency (need GABA, ceiling effect); barbiturates increase open duration and can gate directly.
Benzodiazepines are first-line for status epilepticus; response falls as seizures persist (receptor internalization).
Vigabatrin inhibits GABA transaminase (visual field loss risk); tiagabine blocks GABA reuptake.
Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist for spasticity; abrupt intrathecal withdrawal is an emergency.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines but can precipitate seizures in chronic users.

test.q: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptors by increasing:
test.explain: Benzodiazepines increase how often the channel opens; barbiturates increase how long it stays open.

test.q: Which ion flows through GABA-A receptors?
test.explain: GABA-A is a chloride channel; Cl- entry usually hyperpolarizes the neuron.

test.q: Why are barbiturates more dangerous in overdose than benzodiazepines?
choices: At high levels they open GABA-A channels even without GABA
They do not cross the blood-brain barrier
test.explain: Direct gating means no ceiling effect, so severe respiratory depression can occur.

test.q: Which drug is first-line for a seizure lasting longer than five minutes?
choices: Ethosuximide, as used for absence seizures
Baclofen, to relax the convulsing muscles
A benzodiazepine such as lorazepam or midazolam
Vigabatrin, as used for infantile spasms
test.explain: Benzodiazepines are first-line for status epilepticus.

test.q: Vigabatrin works by:
test.explain: Vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA-T, the enzyme that breaks down GABA.

test.q: A major adverse effect of vigabatrin that needs monitoring is:
choices: Kidney stones from carbonic anhydrase block
Sensorineural hearing loss at high pitches
test.explain: Vigabatrin can cause irreversible concentric visual field constriction.

test.q: Baclofen treats spasticity by acting on:
test.explain: Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.

test.q: Zolpidem's sedative effect relates mainly to which GABA-A subunit?
test.explain: Z-drugs prefer α1-containing receptors, which mediate sedation.

test.q: Name the antagonist that blocks the benzodiazepine binding site.
test.explain: Flumazenil competitively blocks the benzodiazepine site; it can provoke seizures in chronic users.

test.q: Tiagabine raises synaptic GABA by blocking the reuptake transporter GAT-___.
test.explain: Tiagabine inhibits GAT-1.

test.q: What is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain?
test.explain: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter in the brain; glycine plays that role more in the spinal cord and brainstem.

kidTest.q: GABA tells brain cells to…
kidTest.explain: GABA is the brain's main calming signal.

kidTest.q: The calming chemical in the brain is called ___.
kidTest.explain: GABA helps brain cells stay calm.

kidTest.q: Medicines that help GABA are like…
choices: Turning up the 'shh, slow down' voice
Turning up the 'wake up, go fast' voice
Turning on a loud fire alarm in your head
kidTest.explain: They make GABA's calming effect stronger.

kidTest.q: A side effect doctors watch for is…
kidTest.explain: Too much calming can make people very sleepy and slow breathing.

kidTest.q: Baclofen helps muscles that are…
kidTest.explain: Baclofen helps relax tight, stiff muscles (spasticity).

advancedTest.q: Why does benzodiazepine efficacy decline as status epilepticus continues?
choices: Benzodiazepines are metabolized much faster by the liver during seizures
Synaptic γ2-containing GABA-A receptors are internalized while NMDA receptors increase at the surface
The blood–brain barrier closes during status and keeps the drug out of the brain
GABA synthesis falls sharply, leaving little for the drug to enhance
advancedTest.explain: The receptor trafficking hypothesis explains time-dependent pharmacoresistance.

advancedTest.q: Why is GABA often depolarizing in neonatal neurons?
choices: GABA-A receptors are absent until after the first year of life
Neonatal neurons lack chloride, so cations carry the GABA current
GABA binds glutamate receptors on immature neurons and excites them
High NKCC1 and low KCC2 raise intracellular Cl-
advancedTest.explain: High intracellular chloride reverses the Cl- gradient, so opening GABA-A channels depolarizes the cell.

advancedTest.q: A patient with an intrathecal baclofen pump presents with fever, severe rebound spasticity, itching and tachycardia after a refill visit. Most likely:
advancedTest.explain: Interrupted intrathecal baclofen causes a withdrawal syndrome that can be fatal; restore delivery urgently.

advancedTest.q: Name the syndrome of acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and cardiac failure from prolonged high-rate propofol infusions.
advancedTest.explain: Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) is a recognized risk in refractory status epilepticus.

lessons.title: Glutamate-Targeting Drugs

levels.kid:
Brain cells have a "go" signal too. The main one is a chemical called glutamate.

Glutamate is very useful. It helps you learn and remember. But too much glutamate is like a car with the gas pedal stuck down. Cells can fire too much and cause seizures. If it goes on a long time, it can even hurt the cells.

Some medicines gently press the brakes on glutamate. One helps some seizures. Another helps people with memory problems. Another slows a muscle disease a little.

Doctors use them carefully, because we still need some glutamate to think!
levels.hs:
**Glutamate** is the brain's main excitatory ("go") neurotransmitter. It acts on several receptors:
- **AMPA receptors**: fast excitation, the everyday workhorse.
- **NMDA receptors**: need both glutamate and a depolarized cell to open, and let in calcium. They are key for learning and memory.
- **Kainate** and **metabotropic** (G-protein) glutamate receptors.

Too much glutamate overloads neurons with calcium and can kill them, a process called **excitotoxicity**. It plays a role in stroke, trauma and seizures.

**Drugs that reduce glutamate signaling**
- **Perampanel**: blocks AMPA receptors; used for focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. It can cause irritability or aggression, so families are warned.
- **Topiramate**: several actions, including blocking AMPA/kainate receptors and sodium channels. Used for epilepsy and migraine prevention. Side effects include slowed thinking, word-finding trouble, tingling and kidney stones.
- **Memantine**: blocks NMDA receptors only when they are overactive; used in moderate to severe Alzheimer disease.
- **Riluzole**: reduces glutamate release; modestly extends survival in ALS.
- **Levetiracetam**: binds a vesicle protein (SV2A) and reduces neurotransmitter release; one of the most used antiseizure drugs. Mood changes and irritability are its main side effects.

The challenge: block harmful overactivity without blocking the glutamate signaling we need for normal thinking.
levels.college:
**Ionotropic glutamate receptors**
- **AMPA** (GluA1-4): Na+/K+ channels mediating fast EPSPs; GluA2 with RNA editing (Q/R site) makes them Ca2+-impermeable.
- **NMDA** (GluN1 with GluN2A-D): require glutamate plus the co-agonist glycine or D-serine, and depolarization to expel the **voltage-dependent Mg2+ block**. They are Ca2+-permeable coincidence detectors underlying LTP.
- **Kainate** (GluK1-5): pre- and postsynaptic modulators.
**Metabotropic** mGluR1-8 are G-protein coupled (groups I-III).

**Antiseizure drugs**
- **Perampanel**: noncompetitive (allosteric) AMPA antagonist; long half-life; psychiatric effects (hostility, aggression) carry a boxed warning; dizziness and falls.
- **Topiramate**: blocks Na+ channels, enhances GABA-A, antagonizes AMPA/kainate and weakly inhibits carbonic anhydrase. Adverse effects: cognitive slowing and word-finding difficulty, paresthesias, weight loss, calcium phosphate kidney stones, metabolic acidosis, oligohidrosis with hyperthermia in children, and acute angle-closure glaucoma. Teratogenic (oral clefts).
- **Felbamate**: NMDA (GluN2B) antagonism among other actions; effective in Lennox-Gastaut but restricted because of aplastic anemia and hepatic failure.
- **Levetiracetam/brivaracetam**: bind synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A), reducing vesicle release; renal clearance, few interactions; behavioral adverse effects.

**Neuroprotective and other agents**
- **Memantine**: low-affinity, uncompetitive, voltage-dependent NMDA channel blocker with fast off-rate, preferentially blocking tonic pathological activation while sparing phasic physiological signaling.
dissociative anesthesia, analgesia, preserved airway reflexes and sympathetic tone.
- **Riluzole**: reduces presynaptic glutamate release (Na+ channel inhibition); modest survival benefit in ALS; monitor liver enzymes.
- **Excitotoxicity cascade**: NMDA-mediated Ca2+ overload activates calpains, nNOS, mitochondrial failure and cell death.

**Why NMDA neuroprotection failed in stroke trials**: narrow time windows, blocking physiological signaling, intolerable psychotomimetic effects, and NMDA's dual role (synaptic GluN2A prosurvival vs extrasynaptic GluN2B prodeath signaling).
levels.phd:
**The neuroprotection paradox.** Dozens of NMDA antagonists protected neurons in rodent ischemia but failed in human stroke and TBI trials. Explanations include: drugs given hours late after excitotoxic Ca2+ loads had already occurred; NMDA receptors being required for recovery and plasticity; and receptor location. **Synaptic** GluN2A-rich receptors activate CREB and prosurvival signaling, whereas **extrasynaptic** GluN2B-rich receptors couple to CREB shut-off and death signaling, including via the PSD-95–nNOS complex. **Nerinetide** (a peptide disrupting PSD-95 coupling) improved outcomes in a subgroup without alteplase in ESCAPE-NA1, but the effect was abolished by alteplase-generated plasmin cleaving the peptide, and ESCAPE-NEXT did not confirm benefit.

**Memantine's kinetics.** As an uncompetitive open-channel blocker, memantine enters only open channels. Its moderate affinity and fast unblocking let it leave during strong, brief synaptic activation (similar to Mg2+) but occupy channels during prolonged low-level activation, the "tonic noise" hypothesized in Alzheimer disease.

**AMPA antagonism.** Perampanel binds a site at the linker between the ligand-binding domain and the transmembrane region, stabilizing a closed conformation; this noncompetitive action holds even with high synaptic glutamate, an advantage during seizures. The narrow therapeutic window reflects AMPA receptors' ubiquity.

**SV2A biology.** SV2A regulates vesicle priming and the readily releasable pool; levetiracetam effects appear activity-dependent, entering recycling vesicles during high-frequency firing. SV2A PET ligands (such as UCB-J) now quantify synaptic density in vivo in epilepsy and neurodegeneration.

**Glutamate transport.** EAAT2 (GLT-1) on astrocytes clears most synaptic glutamate; its loss in ALS motor cortex and spinal cord supports excitotoxic models of motor neuron death. Ceftriaxone, which upregulates GLT-1 in preclinical work, failed in a phase III ALS trial, a cautionary example of target engagement versus clinical benefit.
levels.expert:
**Using glutamate-targeting antiseizure drugs well**

**Levetiracetam** is the default for many: broad spectrum, IV formulation, renal clearance with dose adjustment in kidney disease, and essentially no hepatic interactions. That is why it dominates neurosurgical seizure prophylaxis and ICU use. The trade-off is behavioral: irritability, low mood, anxiety and, rarely, psychosis. Ask about mood at every visit; switching to brivaracetam or lamotrigine often helps. In patients with a psychiatric history, think twice.

**Topiramate**: counsel about cognitive slowing, paresthesias, kidney stones and the rare but sight-threatening **acute angle-closure glaucoma** (sudden eye pain, blurred vision, usually within the first month): stop the drug and get urgent ophthalmology. Avoid in people with prior stones or those on other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Reduces effectiveness of some hormonal contraceptives at higher exposures; teratogenic.

**Perampanel**: warn the family about irritability and aggression, start low at bedtime, and coordinate with enzyme-inducing drugs that lower its level.

**Felbamate**: reserved for refractory Lennox-Gastaut with informed consent and blood and liver monitoring.

**Memantine**: modest benefit in moderate-severe Alzheimer disease, often combined with a cholinesterase inhibitor; dizziness and confusion are the usual issues; reduce in severe renal impairment.

**Riluzole in ALS**: modest survival benefit; check liver enzymes and blood counts. Edaravone (a free-radical scavenger) is a separate option.

modern data in ventilated patients show it does not meaningfully raise ICP when ventilation is controlled, and it supports blood pressure. It is a useful agent in refractory status epilepticus.

**Pitfall**: blaming every mood change on the epilepsy. Antiseizure drugs, especially levetiracetam, perampanel and topiramate, are frequent culprits.

keyPoints: Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter (AMPA, NMDA, kainate, metabotropic receptors).
Excessive NMDA-mediated Ca2+ entry causes excitotoxicity.
Perampanel is a noncompetitive AMPA antagonist; watch for aggression/irritability.
Topiramate has multiple mechanisms; adverse effects include cognitive slowing, kidney stones and angle-closure glaucoma.
Memantine is a low-affinity uncompetitive NMDA blocker for Alzheimer disease; riluzole reduces glutamate release in ALS.
Levetiracetam binds SV2A; few interactions but behavioral side effects.

test.q: Which receptor needs both glutamate and depolarization (to remove Mg2+) before it opens?
test.explain: NMDA receptors are coincidence detectors with a voltage-dependent Mg2+ block.

test.q: Perampanel's mechanism is:
test.explain: Perampanel allosterically blocks AMPA receptors.

test.q: Which adverse effect is most associated with perampanel?
test.explain: Psychiatric effects such as hostility and aggression carry a boxed warning.

test.q: Topiramate can cause kidney stones because it:
test.explain: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes metabolic acidosis and favors calcium phosphate stones.

test.q: Memantine is used for:
test.explain: Memantine, an NMDA blocker, gives modest benefit in moderate-severe Alzheimer disease.

test.q: Riluzole is used in which disease?
test.explain: Riluzole reduces glutamate release and modestly extends survival in ALS.

test.q: Levetiracetam binds which target?
test.explain: Levetiracetam binds synaptic vesicle protein 2A.

test.q: A sudden painful red eye with blurred vision weeks after starting topiramate suggests:
test.explain: Topiramate can cause acute angle-closure glaucoma; stop it and get urgent eye care.

test.q: What is the term for neuron death caused by excessive glutamate stimulation?
test.explain: Excitotoxicity is driven largely by NMDA-mediated Ca2+ overload.

test.q: NMDA receptors at rest are blocked by a ___ ion that leaves when the cell depolarizes.
test.explain: The voltage-dependent Mg2+ block makes NMDA receptors coincidence detectors.

test.q: Name the NMDA channel blocker used in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease.
test.explain: Memantine is a low-affinity, fast-off NMDA channel blocker.

kidTest.q: Glutamate is a ___ signal.
kidTest.explain: Glutamate is the brain's main 'go' (excitatory) signal.

kidTest.q: Too much glutamate is like…
kidTest.explain: Too much 'go' makes cells fire too much.

kidTest.q: Glutamate helps you…
kidTest.explain: Glutamate is key for learning and memory.

kidTest.q: The brain's main 'go' chemical is ___.
kidTest.explain: Glutamate excites brain cells.

kidTest.q: Why don't doctors block ALL glutamate?
choices: It is not in the brain
kidTest.explain: Normal glutamate signaling is needed for thinking and memory.

advancedTest.q: Why is memantine well tolerated even though it blocks NMDA channels?
choices: Memantine has limited brain penetration and acts mainly on peripheral NMDA receptors
Its low affinity and fast off-rate spare normal phasic synaptic activity
Memantine is a GABA-A agonist that balances its NMDA blocking effect
It actually blocks AMPA receptors instead of NMDA receptors at synapses
advancedTest.explain: Fast unblocking lets memantine leave during strong synaptic activity, like Mg2+, while damping tonic activation.

advancedTest.q: Which hypothesis explains why NMDA receptor location matters for neuronal survival?
choices: NMDA receptors are harmful wherever they sit on the neuron
NMDA receptors are found mainly in glia, so neuronal location is irrelevant
Location affects mainly AMPA receptors, which sit beside the NMDA receptors
Synaptic GluN2A receptors signal survival, extrasynaptic GluN2B receptors signal death
advancedTest.explain: Synaptic vs extrasynaptic NMDA signaling has opposite effects on CREB and survival pathways.

advancedTest.q: A patient on levetiracetam after tumor resection develops marked irritability and low mood. A reasonable step is:
choices: Ignore it as a normal part of recovery from the surgery
Consider switching to an alternative such as brivaracetam or lamotrigine
Double the dose, since mood symptoms mean poor seizure control
Add perampanel to improve mood and seizure control together
advancedTest.explain: Behavioral effects are the main limitation of levetiracetam; switching often helps.

advancedTest.q: Name the main astrocytic glutamate transporter (EAAT2 in humans; its rodent name).
advancedTest.explain: EAAT2/GLT-1 clears most synaptic glutamate; its loss is implicated in ALS.

lessons.title: Local & General Anesthetics

levels.kid:
Have you ever had a numbing shot at the dentist? That is a local anesthetic. It only works in one small spot.

Nerves carry "ouch" messages to your brain like runners passing a note. The numbing medicine blocks the runners' path, so the note never arrives. You don't feel the pain, even though you are awake.

A general anesthetic is different. It puts your whole brain into a very deep, safe sleep for surgery. You don't feel, move or remember anything.

A special doctor called an anesthesiologist watches your breathing and heart the whole time and wakes you up when it's done.
levels.hs:
**Local anesthetics** (lidocaine, bupivacaine) numb one area by blocking **voltage-gated sodium channels** inside nerve fibers. With no sodium entry, no action potential travels, so the pain signal never reaches the brain.
- Small pain fibers are blocked first; touch, pressure and movement fade later.
- They work less well in infected (acidic) tissue, because less drug can enter the nerve.
- **Epinephrine** is often added: it narrows blood vessels, keeps the drug in place longer and reduces bleeding.
- Two families: **esters** (such as procaine, tetracaine) and **amides** (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine). Trick: amides have two "i"s in their names.
- Too much reaching the bloodstream causes **local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)**: ringing ears, metallic taste, seizures, then heart rhythm problems. Lipid emulsion is a treatment.

**General anesthesia** produces unconsciousness, amnesia, no movement and blunted stress responses.
- **IV agents**: propofol (fast on, fast off), etomidate (keeps blood pressure stable).
- **Inhaled agents**: sevoflurane, desflurane, isoflurane.
- Many enhance GABA-A receptors.

**Malignant hyperthermia** is a rare inherited reaction to inhaled agents and succinylcholine: muscles become rigid, temperature and CO2 soar. **Dantrolene** is the antidote.
levels.college:
**Local anesthetics (LAs)** are weak bases with a lipophilic aromatic ring, an intermediate ester or amide link and a tertiary amine. The **uncharged** form crosses the membrane; inside, the **charged** form binds the Nav pore from the cytoplasmic side, preferentially in open/inactivated states (use-dependent block). Lower pKa means more uncharged drug at body pH and faster onset; lipid solubility determines potency; protein binding correlates with duration.

**Differential block**: small myelinated Aδ and unmyelinated C fibers and preganglionic B fibers block before large Aα motor fibers. Sequence: autonomic and pain, then temperature, touch, pressure and finally motor.

**Metabolism**: esters by plasma butyrylcholinesterase (para-aminobenzoic acid metabolite, the usual cause of true allergy); amides by the liver.

**LAST**: CNS excitation (perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation, seizures) then CNS depression and cardiovascular collapse; bupivacaine is especially cardiotoxic because it dissociates slowly from cardiac Na+ channels. Management: stop injection, airway, benzodiazepines for seizures, **20% lipid emulsion**, modified ACLS (avoid vasopressin, use reduced epinephrine).

**General anesthetics**
- **Potency** of inhaled agents is expressed as **MAC** (minimum alveolar concentration at which half of patients do not move to incision). Lower MAC = more potent.
- **Speed**: low blood:gas partition coefficient = faster induction and emergence (desflurane, sevoflurane fastest).
- **Dexmedetomidine** (α2 agonist) gives arousable sedation without respiratory depression.
- **Etomidate** inhibits 11β-hydroxylase (adrenal suppression); **propofol** causes hypotension and is antiemetic.

**Malignant hyperthermia**: RYR1 (or CACNA1S) variants cause uncontrolled sarcoplasmic Ca2+ release with triggering agents; rising end-tidal CO2 is often the earliest sign. Treatment: stop triggers, dantrolene (RyR1 antagonist), cooling, treat hyperkalemia.
levels.phd:
**How general anesthetics make consciousness disappear** remains incompletely understood. The Meyer-Overton correlation between lipid solubility and potency once suggested a nonspecific lipid mechanism; Franks and Lieb showed anesthetics inhibit a lipid-free protein (firefly luciferase) with similar potency ordering, shifting focus to protein targets. Knock-in mice with GABA-A β3 N265M mutations become insensitive to propofol and etomidate immobility and hypnosis, while β2 N265S affects sedation, establishing specific receptor sites.

**Circuits and networks.** Anesthetics act on sleep-wake circuitry (for example, potentiating GABAergic output from the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus onto arousal nuclei) but also disrupt corticocortical and thalamocortical integration. Propofol produces frontal alpha oscillations with slow waves, reflecting hyperpolarized thalamocortical loops. Measures such as perturbational complexity (TMS-evoked EEG) distinguish unconscious states and track integrated information. Immobility from volatile agents is mediated largely at the spinal cord, not the brain, explaining why MAC is a spinal measure.

**Two-pore-domain K+ channels.** TREK-1 and TASK channels are activated by volatile anesthetics; TREK-1 knockout mice show reduced sensitivity. Recent work suggests anesthetics disrupt lipid rafts, releasing phospholipase D2 that generates phosphatidic acid to open TREK-1, reviving a role for membranes via a protein pathway.

**Developmental neurotoxicity.** Animal studies showed anesthetic-induced apoptosis in developing brains; human studies (GAS trial: regional versus general anesthesia in infants; PANDA) found no meaningful difference in neurodevelopmental outcome after a single short anesthetic, though questions remain for repeated or prolonged exposure.

**Local anesthetic structural biology.** Cryo-EM confirms LAs bind the central cavity beneath the selectivity filter, interacting with DIV-S6 phenylalanine. Subtype-selective Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 inhibitors (Nav1.8 inhibitor suzetrigine approved for acute pain in 2025) target pain without CNS or cardiac block, informed by human genetics of congenital insensitivity to pain.
levels.expert:
**Anesthesia for neurosurgery is brain physiology management.**

**Cerebral effects**
- **Propofol** lowers cerebral metabolic rate (CMRO2), cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure, with coupling preserved. Ideal for patients with raised ICP.
- **Volatile agents** also reduce metabolism but directly **vasodilate** cerebral vessels, raising blood volume and ICP in a dose-dependent way and impairing autoregulation at higher concentrations. In a tight brain, the surgeon may ask to switch to total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA).
- **Dexmedetomidine** is valued in **awake craniotomy** for language mapping: patients are sedated yet can cooperate, with minimal respiratory depression.

**Neuromonitoring.** Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) are highly sensitive to volatile agents and abolished by neuromuscular blockade, so spine and tumor surgery with MEP monitoring generally uses propofol-opioid TIVA with no paralytic after intubation. Somatosensory evoked potentials are less sensitive but still depressed by volatiles.

**Scalp blocks and local infiltration.** Long-acting amide blocks of the scalp nerves blunt pin-fixation responses and reduce postoperative pain. Calculate the total local anesthetic across all sites; LAST risk climbs with multiple injections. Keep lipid emulsion available whenever large blocks are performed.

**Malignant hyperthermia readiness.** Ask about family history of anesthetic problems; certain myopathies (central core disease, King-Denborough) carry risk. A clean (trigger-free) TIVA technique is standard for susceptible patients, and dantrolene must be immediately available.

**Pitfalls**
- Etomidate in a septic patient: single-dose adrenal suppression is real, though clinical significance is debated.
- Local anesthetic "allergy" is usually a vasovagal or epinephrine reaction; true allergy is mostly to esters (PABA), so an amide can usually be chosen.
- Spinal anesthesia in a patient with raised ICP risks herniation from CSF pressure gradients.

keyPoints: Local anesthetics block Na+ channels from inside; the uncharged form crosses the membrane, the charged form binds.
Small pain and autonomic fibers block before large motor fibers.
Esters are metabolized by plasma cholinesterase (PABA allergy); amides by the liver (two i's in the name).
LAST: CNS symptoms then cardiac collapse; bupivacaine most cardiotoxic; treat with lipid emulsion.
MAC measures inhaled anesthetic potency; low blood:gas solubility means fast onset and offset.
Propofol lowers ICP; volatile agents vasodilate cerebral vessels; malignant hyperthermia is treated with dantrolene.

test.q: Local anesthetics block which channel?
test.explain: They block Nav channels from inside the axon, stopping action potentials.

test.q: Which fibers are blocked first by local anesthetics?
test.explain: Small-diameter fibers are blocked first.

test.q: Why are local anesthetics less effective in infected tissue?
choices: Infection destroys the drug chemically before it can reach the nerve
Acidic tissue keeps more drug in the charged form that cannot cross membranes
Bacteria break the drug down and use it as an energy source
Blood flow stops completely in infected tissue, so no drug arrives
test.explain: Low pH ionizes the weak base, reducing entry into nerves.

test.q: Which drug is an amide local anesthetic?
test.explain: Bupivacaine has two i's: an amide. The others are esters.

test.q: A lower MAC value means an inhaled anesthetic is:
test.explain: MAC is inversely related to potency.

test.q: Which IV anesthetic suppresses adrenal steroid synthesis?
test.explain: Etomidate inhibits 11β-hydroxylase.

test.q: Which anesthetic lowers cerebral metabolism and intracranial pressure, making it favored in neurosurgery?
test.explain: Propofol reduces CMRO2, cerebral blood flow and ICP.

test.q: Earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia under anesthesia is often:
test.explain: Hypermetabolism raises CO2 production first; fever may come later.

test.q: Name the antidote for malignant hyperthermia.
test.explain: Dantrolene blocks RyR1 calcium release in skeletal muscle.

test.q: Severe local anesthetic systemic toxicity is treated with intravenous ___ emulsion.
test.explain: Lipid emulsion acts as a 'lipid sink' and supports the heart.

test.q: Which alpha-2 agonist gives arousable sedation, useful in awake craniotomy?
test.explain: Dexmedetomidine sedates with minimal respiratory depression.

kidTest.q: A numbing shot at the dentist works…
kidTest.explain: Local anesthetics numb a small area.

kidTest.q: General anesthesia makes you…
choices: Run super fast around the room
Super hungry for a big snack
kidTest.explain: General anesthesia keeps your brain unaware during surgery.

kidTest.q: Who watches you during surgery sleep?
choices: An airplane pilot in the room
A chef from the hospital kitchen
kidTest.explain: Anesthesiologists watch breathing and heart.

kidTest.q: Numbing medicine stops ___ messages from reaching the brain.
kidTest.explain: It blocks the nerve signal carrying pain.

kidTest.q: When you get a numbing shot, are you awake?
kidTest.explain: Local anesthesia numbs one spot; you stay awake.

advancedTest.q: Why is bupivacaine more cardiotoxic than lidocaine?
choices: It is an ester, so plasma esterases convert it to a cardiotoxin
It dissociates slowly from cardiac Na+ channels
It is not protein-bound, so free levels in the heart rise quickly
It acts mainly through cardiac calcium channels rather than Na+ channels
advancedTest.explain: Slow unbinding ('fast-in, slow-out') causes cumulative cardiac Na+ channel block.

advancedTest.q: During spine surgery with MEP monitoring, the anesthesiologist most likely uses:
choices: High-concentration volatile anesthesia with ongoing neuromuscular blockade
advancedTest.explain: Volatiles and paralytics suppress MEPs; propofol-based TIVA preserves them.

advancedTest.q: Evidence that volatile anesthetic immobility is spinally mediated came from:
choices: Firefly luciferase activity assays in vitro
Goat studies isolating brain from spinal circulation
PET imaging of brain glucose uptake in humans
Knockout mice lacking the TREK-1 K+ channel
advancedTest.explain: Selective delivery to the brain in goats required much higher concentrations to stop movement.

advancedTest.q: Which mouse mutation in GABA-A β3 made animals insensitive to propofol and etomidate? (residue code)
advancedTest.explain: The β3 N265M knock-in showed specific receptor targets for these anesthetics.

lessons.title: Adverse Effects & Interactions

levels.kid:
Every medicine has a job, but sometimes it does extra things we don't want. Those are called side effects.

Some seizure medicines can make you dizzy or sleepy. A few can cause a rash, so doctors say: if you see a new rash, tell a grown-up right away!

Medicines can also bump into each other, like two kids trying to use the same swing. One medicine can make another one weaker or stronger. That's why doctors always ask, "What other medicines do you take?"

And you should never stop seizure medicine suddenly by yourself, because seizures can come back.
levels.hs:
Antiseizure medications (ASMs) are often taken for years, so side effects and interactions matter a lot.

**Common side effects**: sleepiness, dizziness, unsteady walking, double vision. These are usually dose-related.

**Serious, rarer reactions**
- **Severe skin rashes** (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) with carbamazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine. A new rash with fever, sores in the mouth or blistering is an emergency.
- **Liver injury and pancreatitis** with valproate.
- **Low sodium** with carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine.
- **Mood changes** with levetiracetam.
- **Birth defects**: valproate has the highest risk (neural tube defects and lower IQ in children exposed before birth), so it is avoided in people who could become pregnant when possible.

**Drug interactions**
- **Enzyme inducers** (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) speed up the liver's breakdown of other drugs. They can make birth control pills and blood thinners like warfarin less effective.
- **Valproate** slows the breakdown of lamotrigine, raising its level and the risk of rash.
- Some antibiotics (carbapenems) sharply lower valproate levels.
- Combining sedating drugs (benzodiazepines, opioids, alcohol) can dangerously slow breathing.

**Never stop suddenly**: abrupt withdrawal can trigger seizures or status epilepticus.
levels.college:
**Pharmacokinetic interactions** revolve around cytochrome P450 (CYP) and UGT enzymes.
- **Strong inducers**: carbamazepine (CYP3A4, also autoinduction), phenytoin, phenobarbital/primidone. They lower levels of hormonal contraceptives, warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants, many chemotherapy agents, immunosuppressants and other ASMs. Oxcarbazepine, eslicarbazepine and topiramate (at higher exposure) are weaker inducers of contraceptive metabolism.
- **Inhibitor**: valproate inhibits UGT and epoxide hydrolase, raising lamotrigine and carbamazepine-epoxide levels; it also displaces phenytoin from albumin.
- **Carbapenems** reduce valproate levels dramatically within a day (inhibiting acylpeptide hydrolase that recycles valproate glucuronide), causing breakthrough seizures.
- **Estrogen** induces lamotrigine glucuronidation, so lamotrigine levels fall on combined contraceptives and in pregnancy.
- **Low-interaction ASMs**: levetiracetam, lacosamide, gabapentin, pregabalin (renal clearance).

**Idiosyncratic reactions**
- **SJS/TEN**: aromatic ASMs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital); highest risk in the first two months; HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine.
- **DRESS** (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms): fever, rash, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, weeks after starting.
- **Valproate**: hepatotoxicity (highest in young children on multiple ASMs and in POLG mitochondrial disease), pancreatitis, hyperammonemic encephalopathy (treat with L-carnitine), thrombocytopenia, tremor, weight gain, hair loss, polycystic ovary features.
- **Felbamate**: aplastic anemia; **vigabatrin**: visual field loss.

**Teratogenicity**: valproate (neural tube defects, cognitive and autism-spectrum effects; strict pregnancy-prevention programs), topiramate (oral clefts, growth restriction), phenobarbital and phenytoin (fetal hydantoin syndrome). Lamotrigine and levetiracetam carry the lowest known risk. Folic acid supplementation is advised.

**Bone health**: enzyme inducers accelerate vitamin D catabolism, causing osteoporosis and osteomalacia with long-term use.
levels.phd:
**Pharmacogenomics of hypersensitivity.** HLA-B*15:02 presents carbamazepine directly to T-cell receptors via the p-i (pharmacological interaction with immune receptors) concept, rather than as a hapten, explaining reactions on first exposure without prior sensitization. The allele's frequency varies widely: common in Han Chinese, Thai and Malaysian populations, rare in Japanese and Korean populations, where HLA-A*31:01 is more relevant. The negative predictive value is high but positive predictive value low, a classic screening trade-off. **CYP2C9*3** and **HLA-B*15:02** together predict phenytoin-related severe cutaneous reactions, reflecting both drug exposure and immune presentation.

**Valproate hepatotoxicity mechanisms.** Valproate is a branched fatty acid metabolized by β-oxidation and CYP pathways; the 4-ene metabolite inhibits mitochondrial β-oxidation, and valproyl-CoA depletes CoA and carnitine. In **POLG** mutations (Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome), the risk of fatal liver failure is so high that POLG testing precedes valproate in suspected mitochondrial disease. Hyperammonemia arises from carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I inhibition via N-acetylglutamate depletion.

**Developmental neurotoxicity.** Prospective cohorts (NEAD, UK and Ireland Epilepsy and Pregnancy Register, EURAP) show dose-dependent major malformations and reduced verbal IQ after in utero valproate. Proposed mechanisms include histone deacetylase inhibition altering developmental gene expression and folate antagonism. Concern has extended to paternal exposure, with regulators advising precautions, though causality remains debated.

**Drug-drug interaction modeling.** Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models predict induction magnitude for new agents; pregnane X receptor (PXR) and constitutive androstane receptor (CAR) activation explain carbamazepine's broad induction of CYP3A4, CYP2C, UGT and P-glycoprotein. Induction develops and resolves over about two weeks because it depends on enzyme synthesis and turnover.

**Cognitive and behavioral burden.** Pooled analyses link levetiracetam to irritability via possible SV2A effects in limbic circuits; genetic variation in dopaminergic pathways may modulate risk, an active area of personalized prescribing research.
levels.expert:
**How an attending thinks about ASM safety**

**Before prescribing**: Is this person able to become pregnant? What else do they take? Ancestry (HLA screening)? Liver, kidney, sodium, blood counts, psychiatric history, bone health?

**The "rash conversation"**: for lamotrigine, carbamazepine and phenytoin, tell patients to stop and seek care immediately for rash with fever, mucosal sores, blistering or skin pain. Restarting lamotrigine after a pause means re-titrating from the beginning.

**Hyponatremia**: oxcarbazepine more than carbamazepine; older adults on diuretics are at highest risk. New confusion or more seizures in an older patient on oxcarbazepine: check sodium first.

**Valproate**: confusion or lethargy with a normal liver panel can be hyperammonemic encephalopathy; check ammonia. Avoid in suspected mitochondrial disease until POLG is tested.

**Inducers in neurosurgical and oncology patients**: phenytoin can cut levels of dexamethasone and many chemotherapies, and dexamethasone in turn can lower phenytoin. That is a major reason levetiracetam replaced phenytoin for glioma patients.

**ICU traps**
- Starting meropenem in a patient on valproate: expect a level collapse within a day; choose another antibiotic or switch the ASM.
- Benzodiazepines plus opioids in a postoperative patient: monitor breathing.
- Some drugs lower the seizure threshold: bupropion, tramadol, high-exposure cefepime (especially with renal failure), carbapenems (imipenem most), fluoroquinolones.

**Women's health**: inducers make hormonal contraceptives unreliable; levonorgestrel IUD or copper IUD avoids the problem. Lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy and rise after delivery, so monitor levels each trimester and adjust postpartum to avoid toxicity.

**Withdrawal**: never stop abruptly; after a seizure-free period, taper slowly with a plan, and counsel on driving rules during and after the taper.

keyPoints: Common dose-related ASM effects: sedation, dizziness, ataxia, diplopia.
Aromatic ASMs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) can cause SJS/TEN and DRESS.
Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) lower contraceptive, warfarin and chemotherapy levels.
Valproate raises lamotrigine levels; carbapenems sharply lower valproate levels.
Valproate: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonemia, highest teratogenic risk.
Never stop ASMs abruptly: withdrawal seizures and status epilepticus.

test.q: Which ASM has the highest teratogenic risk?
test.explain: Valproate carries the highest risk of malformations and neurodevelopmental effects.

test.q: Carbamazepine can make hormonal birth control less effective because it:
test.explain: Enzyme induction speeds contraceptive metabolism.

test.q: Adding valproate to lamotrigine:
choices: Lowers lamotrigine levels by inducing its metabolism
Raises lamotrigine levels and rash risk
Has no effect on either drug's levels
Lowers valproate levels and its liver risk
test.explain: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation.

test.q: Which antibiotic class dramatically lowers valproate levels?
test.explain: Carbapenems can drop valproate levels within a day.

test.q: Hyponatremia is most associated with:
test.explain: Oxcarbazepine (and carbamazepine) can cause SIADH-like hyponatremia.

test.q: A confused patient on valproate with normal liver tests should have which test?
test.explain: Valproate can cause hyperammonemic encephalopathy.

test.q: Why is abrupt ASM discontinuation dangerous?
choices: It causes a rebound rash across the body
It can trigger withdrawal seizures or status epilepticus
It causes a dangerous rise in blood pressure
It is not dangerous if the seizures have stopped
test.explain: Sudden withdrawal can provoke seizures, including status epilepticus.

test.q: Which ASM has very few drug interactions and is cleared by the kidney?
test.explain: Levetiracetam is renally cleared and has minimal CYP interactions.

test.q: Name the severe skin reaction with mucosal sores and blistering linked to carbamazepine.
test.explain: SJS/TEN is a medical emergency.

test.q: Valproate hyperammonemia can be treated with L-___.
test.explain: L-carnitine supports fatty acid metabolism and lowers ammonia in valproate toxicity.

test.q: Which vitamin is recommended for people on ASMs who could become pregnant, to lower neural tube defect risk?
test.explain: Folic acid supplementation is advised.

kidTest.q: A side effect is…
choices: The medicine's main job that it was made for
An extra thing a medicine does that we don't want
A kind of vitamin that comes with the pill
kidTest.explain: Side effects are unwanted effects.

kidTest.q: If you get a new rash on a seizure medicine, you should…
choices: Ignore it and hope it goes away
Scratch it until it stops itching
kidTest.explain: Some rashes can be serious, so tell someone right away.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors ask what other medicines you take?
choices: Because they are just being nosy
Just for fun, to pass the time
kidTest.explain: One medicine can make another weaker or stronger.

kidTest.q: You should never ___ seizure medicine suddenly by yourself.
kidTest.explain: Stopping suddenly can bring seizures back.

kidTest.q: Feeling dizzy or sleepy can be…
kidTest.explain: Dizziness and sleepiness are common side effects.

advancedTest.q: A glioma patient on phenytoin and dexamethasone has poor seizure control and less steroid effect. Best explanation?
choices: Phenytoin is cleared by the kidneys, and dexamethasone slows renal function
Mutual induction: phenytoin speeds dexamethasone metabolism and dexamethasone lowers phenytoin
Dexamethasone blocks Na+ channels itself and competes with phenytoin for them
No interaction exists between them; the tumor is simply growing faster
advancedTest.explain: Both drugs induce each other's metabolism; levetiracetam avoids this.

advancedTest.q: Why test POLG before valproate in a child with suspected mitochondrial disease?
choices: POLG status predicts a serious skin rash with valproate
POLG mutations predict severe hyponatremia on valproate
POLG changes kidney clearance, so valproate builds up
POLG mutations confer high risk of fatal valproate liver failure
advancedTest.explain: Alpers-Huttenlocher (POLG) patients are at extreme risk of valproate hepatotoxicity.

advancedTest.q: HLA-B*15:02 screening has which characteristic?
choices: High positive predictive value for carbamazepine reactions
High negative predictive value, low positive predictive value
No predictive value, so screening is no longer recommended
It mainly predicts hyponatremia rather than serious skin reactions
advancedTest.explain: A negative test is reassuring; most carriers still do not react.

advancedTest.q: Name the hypersensitivity syndrome with fever, rash, eosinophilia and organ involvement weeks after starting an ASM (acronym).
accept: drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
advancedTest.explain: DRESS typically appears 2-8 weeks after starting the drug.
